title: A Farewell of a Thousand Arms
story:
The conversation was over, and Krishna rose to take his leave. He had told King Bhishmaka what the gods had decreed on the summit of Mount Sumeru — that Rukmini was Lakshmi herself, born into the house of Kundina to be united with Keshava — and the king had bowed and asked only for wisdom. It was time to go. The kings who had come for the swayamvara were stirring in the city, and Krishna had a journey before him.

But as he stood to go, something happened that Bhishmaka would carry with him for the rest of his life.

The man who had stood before him and spoken of his daughter was suddenly not a man at all.

Bhishmaka looked, and the form before him was vast and quiet and older than the world: the prime and self-sprung Krishna, the one who existed before every beginning, with eyes like red lotuses. He had a thousand feet. A thousand eyes. A thousand arms. The shape of a man, and inside that shape, the shape of everything — every direction at once, every being that breathed, every star the sky had ever held. The king of Kundina stood in the presence of the universe wearing a human face, and he understood, in one blinding instant, who had been sitting in his house and asking for nothing.

Bhishmaka did not speak of his daughter then. He did not speak of the swayamvara, or of his son, or of the kings outside the walls. All of that fell away from him like dust. He bowed low — lower than he had ever bowed to any king, lower than he had bowed even a moment ago when he had begged for forgiveness — and he began to praise.

He praised the glory that stood before him: the self-sprung one, who had no beginning and no cause, who had made himself known in the house of a mortal king. He praised him as the first of all beings, the source from which everything else flowed, the one who was already there before the first dawn and would remain after the last one. The words came out of him slowly at first, then faster, as if the vision had unlocked something in his chest that had been waiting all his life to be spoken. He had thought he was entertaining a guest, a young prince from Mathura who spoke well and carried himself like a king. Now he knew he had been sheltering the Lord of all that exists, and his praise rose and broke over that knowledge like a wave.

And then it was over.

Krishna stood before him again as he had stood before — a young man, gracious, ready to leave. The thousand arms were one pair of arms. The thousand eyes were two. The vision had not been taken away so much as folded back up, the way a vast sky folds into a single point at nightfall.

Bhishmaka straightened slowly, and said nothing. There was nothing left to say. He had been shown what his daughter was, and now he had been shown what her destined husband was, and the two truths together had rearranged his entire world. His son had wanted a grand swayamvara; the gods had wanted something else entirely; and the king, who had spent days anxious and afraid, found that he was no longer afraid of anything.

Outside the palace, the assembled kings were waiting. As Krishna came out of Bhishmaka's presence, they rose and followed him — the kings of the earth, who had come to Kundina to compete for a bride, now following the young man who had claimed her as if drawn by something they could not name. They did not know what Bhishmaka had seen. But they had seen Krishna, and even that was enough to move them.

Bhishmaka watched them go from the doorway of his palace, and what he had seen stayed with him: the self-sprung one, the thousand arms, the red-lotus eyes that held the whole of creation. A king does not forget the day the universe visited his house.
reflection: The cosmic form appears not as a spectacle for a crowd but as a private revelation to one anxious father — the divine answering Bhishmaka's plea for 'eyes of wisdom' by literally showing him what he could not otherwise see. That the vision is followed by Krishna quietly returning to human shape suggests the form is a gift of sight, not a display.
next_story_tease: Once the kings had gone, the swayamvara's true decision passed to Rukmini herself.
hero_scene: Bhishmaka on his knees before Krishna, who stands revealed in his universal form — a thousand feet, a thousand eyes, a thousand arms, eyes like red lotuses — filling the dim hall of Kundina with light while the mortal shape he wore moments ago seems to hang over him like a garment.
visual_elements: light and vastness filling the hall
